text: The applicant group on this route is deliberately non-eu rather than any. A Danish student is an international applicant here and that is not an administrative detail: the route Emirati school-leavers use is a national placement process, and a foreign applicant cannot use it. Recording one route for both would describe a path this site's readers cannot take.
Not binding. The right round for anyone who needs to compare a Danish, Dutch or British offer against this one. NYUAD publishes the date without a year.

This route exists because applying directly is a finding, not a blank. Three of Australia's five tertiary admissions centres state in their own words that an international applicant who is not sitting an Australian Year 12 or the IB inside Australia - or, in Western Australia, who is not a citizen or permanent resident - applies directly to the institution. That is the situation a Danish candidate is in everywhere except New South Wales and the ACT.

AUD 29,710 of living costs for twelve months, plus the first twelve months of the actual course fee, plus about AUD 2,000 of travel from Europe - or, instead of savings, a parent's or partner's documented annual income of at least AUD 87,856, evidenced by official tax documents rather than bank statements. Gathering tax documents from a Danish parent takes longer than gathering a bank statement.
A visa condition, not a university one, and charged separately from tuition. The EHIC and the Danish yellow card are not valid in Australia.
Pacific time is nine hours behind Denmark, so this closes on the morning of 16 January Danish time. It is a deadline for the Winter Session beginning September 2027.
The date that confirms a UBC offer for a Danish IB candidate. Request the electronic transmission of your results from the IB in the spring.
Twelve noon, not midnight. Applies to every applicant with an international or IB qualification, whether the diploma was earned in Denmark or abroad, and whether you are aiming at quota 1 or quota 2.
Sign the application (signature page if you have no MitID)

With MitID you sign inside optagelse.dk. Without MitID, print the signature page, sign it by hand and email or post it to every institution you apply to. Never uploaded. The application is not complete without it.
After the Danish documentation deadline, which is why the results service exists.
There is no later round for IB holders. The 5 July deadline that Danish-qualified applicants use does not apply to you.
The applicant group is non-eu because Hong Kong's categories are local and non-local. A Danish student is non-local, and EU status plays no part.

The latest closing date of any Japanese route recorded here, and the one that fits a Danish school year: predicted grades are settled by then and the result arrives on 24 May, after the examination session. Keio accepts predicted IB grades in as many words.
Ask about apostille and notarisation early. Japanese universities generally want certified documents, and a Danish apostille takes time that a November deadline does not leave.

The Embassy of Japan in Denmark's Study in Japan page refuses plain fetches but was read in a browser on 2026-09-24: it lists two MEXT types for Danish nationals, neither of them the undergraduate scholarship.
Ask the Embassy of Japan in Copenhagen for the Danish dates

Not a published deadline and not anyone's rule. The embassy lists only the Japanese Studies and Research Student types for Danish nationals; if you hold another nationality or want the position in writing, ask in February, because the window itself would fall in April and May 2027, on top of the IB examinations.
The Embassy of Japan in Denmark offers Danish nationals only the Japanese Studies and Research Student scholarships, and both are for students already at university.

MEXT's rule is relative, not a published day: "Recruitment for those arriving in Japan next April is made between April and May of the previous year." For an April 2028 arrival that is April and May 2027. The Embassy of Japan in Denmark, which sets the local dates, does not offer the undergraduate type to Danish nationals, so no day is shown.

The 2027 round required completion by March of the arrival year, or by August where the applicant was entering in the autumn term through direct placement. A Danish gymnasium finishing in June sits between those two conditions, so which one applies is a question for the embassy rather than an assumption to make.
Apply for the dormitory the moment an offer arrives. The private Seoul market needs a large up-front deposit that is impractical to arrange from Denmark.

Treat this as the deliberate alternative to September 2027 rather than as a failure. A March 2028 start means a nine-month gap after the diploma, which is close to the Danish sabbatår most students take anyway, and it puts you in the main Korean intake alongside the domestic cohort rather than in the smaller international one.
Global Korea Scholarship, University Track — the one a Danish citizen can use
This is the only Global Korea Scholarship track open to a Danish citizen, because the UIC Program is the one part of GKS with no country restriction.

No central system: every institution is applied to directly. The Miami University Dolibois European Center is a study-abroad campus for Miami University students and is reached through Miami University, not applied to here.
International students on a student visa are generally not entitled to publicly funded healthcare in New Zealand. The EHIC and the Danish yellow card are not valid here.

The round aimed at applicants from abroad, carrying most English-taught programmes. The 2027 catalogue becomes visible here. University Admissions tells IB students who have not finished the Diploma not to apply in this round.

Closes somewhere between 1 and 15 November 2026 depending on the college, and there is no common date: Macalester 1 November, Amherst 9 November, Bowdoin and Grinnell 15 November. Binding in the strongest sense — Amherst's wording is that you agree not to be an Early Decision candidate anywhere else and, if admitted, to withdraw your applications from other colleges and enrol. Missing it does not cost you the college; it costs you this round, and with it the higher admit rate that is the main reason to accept the binding terms. It also ends any possibility of comparing financial aid offers, which for a Danish family paying from abroad is usually the more expensive loss.
A Danish student pays nonresident tuition at UC for all four years. Residency for tuition is not something an F-1 student acquires by living in California.

Undergraduate courses at universities and colleges in New South Wales and the ACT. Open to international applicants holding an International Baccalaureate Diploma, an Australian Year 12 taken in or outside Australia, or New Zealand NCEA Level 3 - which is what puts a Danish IB candidate inside it.
New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory, plus some institutions in nearby border regions
An OUAC account. No national digital identity is involved, which makes this one of the easier portals in this collection to get into from abroad.
Every state-recognised undergraduate programme in Denmark — universities, university colleges, business academies and the artistic institutions.

Programmes with more applicants than places split their intake into quota 1, allocated on the converted grade average alone, and quota 2, which weighs subject grades, relevant work or education as each institution defines it (Aalborg counts up to twelve months), and sometimes a test or essay. Applying by 15 March puts you in both automatically, provided your average can be converted to the Danish scale.
MitID if you have a Danish CPR number; otherwise log in with your email address. Without MitID you must also send a signed signature page to every institution by 15 March, 12:00.
Create the application in optagelse.dk (MitID, or email if you have no Danish CPR number) and add up to eight programmes in priority order.

Sign every application by 15 March, 12:00. With MitID you sign inside optagelse.dk; without it, print the signature page, sign it by hand and email or post it to each institution — it is never uploaded.

The Embassy of Japan in Denmark's Study in Japan page (read in a browser on 2026-09-24) lists only the Japanese Studies and Research Student types for Danish nationals, so this system has no Danish undergraduate dates to record.

Contact the Japanese diplomatic mission in your own country first. MEXT states that the process and the schedule differ by country and are the mission's to set, so the national page never carries the date you need.

The limit of two applies to numerus fixus programmes specifically; medicine, dentistry, dental hygiene and physiotherapy allow only one application per programme, so not medicine at two universities. Non-selective programmes are not rationed in the same way, and choices are not ranked against each other as they are in Denmark — each application is decided on its own.
Some institutions handle applicants from abroad through their own systems instead, and private institutions are outside it. Check with the institution before assuming Studielink is the route.
Member colleges across the United States and abroad

Denmark has a reputation for English-language higher education, and at master's level that reputation is earned. At bachelor's level it is not. The University of Copenhagen — the country's largest and best known university — teaches all 78 of its bachelor programmes in Danish, and most Danish bachelor's degrees are the same. The English-taught bachelor's offering is real, and it is a specific and fairly narrow set of programmes rather than a choice you can make freely across the country. That is why this site lists the ones it does and not more: the list is short because the reality is.
This is not a rule about you. If you have Danish at A level, or take Studieprøven, the Danish-taught programmes are open to you and the choice becomes much wider.
The Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science, with the institutional examples read from each university's own pages

Quota 1 is national and mechanical: your converted grade average against a published cut-off. Quota 2 is not. The national agency's position is that quota 2 places are allocated "according to criteria published by the institution", which means each institution decides what counts and the criteria genuinely differ between them.

The practical consequence is that there is no general Danish quota 2 strategy to follow, and advice that describes one is describing a single institution. Aalborg states plainly that motivational letters and recommendations are not considered relevant to its quota 2 assessment. Copenhagen Business School requires a motivational essay. Southern Denmark uses an admissions test. Those are three different answers to the same question, all correct, at three universities in one small country.

Check the quota 2 page of the specific programme you want, and treat anything more general than that as background.
There is no single Danish quota 2

A student arriving from the Danish system will look for the table that turns IB points into a local average, and there is not one. Nuffic describes the IB scale and states that a full Diploma is comparable to a VWO diploma, and stops there.

That is not an omission, it is a different design. Dutch admission to a non-selective programme is an entitlement: hold a qualifying diploma, apply by the deadline, and you are in. Where demand exceeds places, the institution runs its own selection on its own criteria, which may weigh grades alongside a motivation letter, a test or an interview. So the question shifts from "what average do I need" to "is this programme selective, and what does that institution actually select on".
There is no Dutch equivalent of the Danish conversion table

Norway passes every test a Danish IB student would apply to a destination. No tuition, an hour from Copenhagen, a qualification that converts cleanly, a familiar culture and favourable SU treatment. And then most students discover that several of the largest universities teach no bachelor programme in English at all.

The useful way to read that is not as a closed door but as a choice with a known price. For an IB applicant, Samordna opptak counts Danish A at grade 3 or better as documented Norwegian, and a Danish speaker reads Norwegian from the first day. Doing so turns Norway from a handful of English-taught programmes into an entire national system, free of charge. A student who will not is choosing between a very small number of options.

Sweden runs two admissions rounds and they are not two chances at the same thing. The first opens in October and closes on 15 January; it is aimed at applicants from abroad and carries the most English-taught programmes. The second closes on 15 April, and the authority says many English-taught programmes are no longer available in it.

For a May 2027 IB candidate the order is reversed. University Admissions says that if you have not completed your IB Diploma you should not apply to the first round, because it cannot assess you in time without the diploma. Your round is the second, with your IB results due to University Admissions by 5 July through the IB Result Service. So shortlist programmes that are still open in the second round, and treat the January round as closed to you unless a programme, like Stockholm School of Economics, says it admits on predicted grades.

Recorded because the route is invisible and not because it has been researched. The UAE's applied-technology sector is the country's answer to the Danish erhvervsakademi — shorter, vocational, employer-facing, and absent from every English-language guide to studying in the Gulf. The presence of an international admissions portal establishes that it is not closed to foreign applicants; it establishes nothing about what an IB Diploma buys there, what it costs, or whether a Danish student would be accepted. Those are open questions and the sectorLandscape entry says so.

The 2026 date is recorded here and deliberately not carried into the 2027 field, which stays not-yet-announced. The second half is the part that decides whether Sorbonne Abu Dhabi is an option at all for a Danish IB student: most of its bachelors are taught in French, and entry to those requires a B2 French qualification — DELF, TEF, TCF or the university's own SELFEE — rather than an IB French grade. That is a named external certificate, and it takes time to obtain.

"Application Dates to be confirmed" is the cleanest not-yet-announced in this Destination — the university has a field for the dates and has left it saying so. The second sentence is the more consequential one for a Danish student: a federal university routes international applicants through a separate channel from the national placement process Emirati school-leavers use, which means the published national timetable is not the one that applies to you, and the office you have to write to is named.

The phrase "during announced application periods" is the whole finding. UAEU's undergraduate admission is organised around windows the ministry opens rather than a standing deadline, and no window is published for 2027 — graduate deadlines are published on the same site and undergraduate ones are not. Recorded as not-published rather than not-yet-announced, because unlike Khalifa and Zayed, UAEU makes no statement that a date is coming. The split between the national stream and the international one is recorded because it determines which of those two answers applies to a Danish applicant, and the page does not say.

The release clause is the part a Danish family needs to read twice. It protects a student who cannot afford the offer, and it does nothing for a student who simply gets a better offer somewhere else — and since NYUAD's aid for non-Emiratis is need-based and it is one of the very few universities outside the United States meeting demonstrated need, that is a live risk rather than a theoretical one. Applying Early Decision here means committing before you can compare.

For an applicant living in Denmark this is the real deadline, and it is not on the admissions page. Birmingham Dubai publishes no application closing date and does publish a visa sponsorship cut-off, which means the binding date for a foreign student is an immigration date rather than an academic one. The September 2027 figure is deliberately left as not-yet-announced: the 2026 date is recorded here so a reader can see roughly where in the year it lands, and it must not be carried across, because both published dates fall within a week or two of the intake and a week's drift would be the whole margin.

Read from the page's second conversion table, 2026-09-23. The page carries two tables and they give different answers for the same diploma score; this is the one headed for applicants other than those who sat the IB in Australia since November 2022, which is the table a Danish candidate is converted on.

Two things make this table dangerous to copy carelessly, and both bite a Danish candidate specifically. First, UAC publishes two schedules on one page. The other one converts an IB Admissions Score (IBAS) in quarter-point steps and is only for candidates who sat the IB in Australia from November 2022 onward; it reads 24.00 to 64.40 and 30.00 to 78.20 where this one reads 24 to 64.60 and 30 to 79.30. A student sitting the May session in Denmark is converted on the whole diploma score, so this is their table and the more precise-looking one is not. Second, the schedule is republished annually. UAC states this one applies to offers made from August 2026, and the values move: reading last year's figures would misplace a student by more than a rank point in the thirties, which is the range where a point decides an offer. The whole table is recorded rather than three sample rows, because a student reading a summary cannot tell which rows were left out.

Recorded as one worked example rather than as an Australian rate, because there is no Australian rate: every institution sets its own and the spread between an arts degree and a health degree at the same university is larger than the spread between universities. UNSW is used because it publishes per unit of credit, which is the only form in which the arithmetic is checkable from Denmark. The reason this matters more in Australia than in Europe is the visa: the financial evidence is the first twelve months of the actual course fee, so the figure a student needs is theirs and not a national average.

Useful mainly for what it lets a student stop worrying about. Australian degree pages quote an entry requirement as a rank - 'lowest selection rank 90' - and a student reading that from Denmark has no way to know whether that rank means the same thing in Perth as in Sydney. It does. The corollary is that the rank is the currency and the IB score is not: a university publishing a selection rank of 90 is asking for roughly an IB 34 on the current schedule, and neither number appears on the other's page.

This is the one place in Australia where a Danish IB candidate is inside a shared admissions system rather than outside it, and it is easy to miss because the page is titled for Year 12 students. Read the list carefully: 'in or outside Australia' qualifies the Australian Year 12 line only. The IB Diploma line carries no location condition at all - which is exactly where UAC differs from VTAC, SATAC and TISC, each of which does restrict the IB to candidates sitting it in Australia or to residents. The same sentence also establishes the rest of the country: outside NSW and the ACT, applying directly to the institution is not a fallback, it is the route.

Recorded for the shape of the cycle rather than for a student sitting the IB in May 2027. These are the dates of the cycle that admits to semester 1 2027, and a Danish candidate finishing in May 2027 is applying for the cycle after it. What carries over is the pattern - open in April, cheaper until the end of September, close in early February - and not the dates. The charge is worth knowing for a separate reason: it is one payment covering every NSW and ACT institution the applicant preferences, where applying directly means one process per university.

The whole UAC calendar is built around the November IB session - its own key-dates sheet has IB results released from Cardiff on 17 December and IB Admissions Scores emailed the next day, which slots neatly into the December and January offer rounds. A May-session candidate's results arrive in July, in the gap between one cycle closing in February and the next opening in April. UAC does not say this is a problem; it says it will not promise a round. The practical reading is that a Danish candidate should expect to be admitted on predicted grades with the result confirmed later, rather than to be considered in a named round. There is a step here nobody mentions: the release has to be authorised by the school's IB coordinator, and it is the school that does it, not the student.

This is the first thing to get right about Ontario and the thing most easily read past. Nearly every date published about applying to an Ontario university is a Group A date, written for a student sitting in an Ontario classroom. A Danish IB student is Group B. Group A's 15 January deadline is therefore not their deadline, and the absence of a Group B deadline is not permission to apply late — it means the university sets the date instead.

The doubled fee is charged for the transcript's origin rather than the applicant's citizenship, which means a Danish IB student pays it whatever passport they hold. UVic also states plainly that its deadlines sit on the programme page rather than the admissions page, which is the same pattern EducationPlannerBC describes for the province as a whole and the reason no BC-wide deadline is recorded here.

This is the institution type nobody mentions to foreigners, and it explains something that otherwise looks like a trick: a Quebec bachelor's degree is often three years rather than four because a Quebec student has already done two years of CEGEP. An IB Diploma holder arriving from abroad enters the university directly and does the longer version. The technical DEC is the genuinely overlooked route — three years, a workplace placement, and an exit into a job rather than into a degree — and it is invisible in every English-language summary of Canadian higher education.

Quebec is a second immigration system stacked on top of the federal one, and this is the single most consequential difference between choosing Montreal and choosing Toronto. The CAQ is a separate application, with its own fee, its own financial test and its own processing time, and it has to be granted before IRCC will issue the study permit. Concordia's advice to apply a month early is this rule in practical form. Whether a Danish student can instead be covered by the Quebec public plan through the social security agreement route could not be established: the RAMQ eligibility pages sit behind a bot-protection challenge and were not readable.

The date to notice is 15 November 2026, which is not an application deadline and is the one that costs the most money. An international student who wants to be considered for UBC's largest awards has to have the whole application in two months before everyone else, in the first term of DP2. The 15 January deadline carries a time zone and a minute, and Pacific time is nine hours behind Denmark, so the Danish moment it closes is the morning of 16 January.
Switzerland splits fees by residence, not by EU citizenship, so a student coming from Denmark pays the higher rate. Only ETH's fees are established here; other universities set their own.

Re-read 2026-09-24: five sittings a year (1月、3月、4月、6月及12月), two specialised-Chinese papers and three basic subjects (mathematics, physics, chemistry), registration at www.csca.cn. The notice says nothing about English-taught programmes or the joint universities. The Danish embassy site still carried no equivalent notice. Read in Chinese.

A new national test, and the most useful thing a Danish IB student needs to know about the Chinese universities. It is quoted from a Chinese embassy notice because csca.cn renders nothing to an automated fetch. Whether the Sino-foreign joint universities require it was not established.

Architectural Technology and Construction Management (Horsens): a 3.5-year, 210 ECTS bachelor with August and February starts, admitting IB holders with Mathematics at C level (passed with at least 2.0), and selecting in quota 2 on a motivational video, grades, work experience and stays abroad.

Every VIA English-taught programme needs English at Danish B level with a weighted average of at least 2.0, or an accepted test (IELTS Academic 6.5, TOEFL iBT 94 before 21 January 2026 or 4.5 after, Cambridge C1 Advanced or C2 Proficiency at 180). A test cannot replace English where it is a specific entry requirement.
The same page lists the Danish qualifications that give access, and they include HF and "IB/EB-Diploma".
An IB qualifies for the Animation Workshop bachelor programmes. Every applicant must document English at Danish B level with a weighted average of at least 2.0, or pass an accepted English test.
The Education degree is "taught partly in English and partly in Danish" according to its own page, so it is not recorded.
Absalon lists the biotechnology diplomingeniør as a professionsbachelor, taught in Danish or English in Kalundborg, with a study start of 1 September.

Zealand's admission page for its English-taught degrees gives the same subject requirements. For ATCM, English B or an accepted test (IELTS Academic 6.5 and others). It ranks applicants on grade average, other education, work, time abroad and higher subject levels, and sometimes interviews. Non-EU applicants pay a EUR 300 application fee.
Royal Danish Academy – Architecture, Design, Conservation
Applicants need English at Danish B level. An IB meets it with English B at SL or higher; otherwise TOEFL, IELTS Academic 6.5 or Cambridge C1/C2 at 180. No dispensation is possible.
The Academy's page for Danish exams lists "Højere forberedelseseksamen uden overbygning" (hf) among the qualifying exams.
An IB counts as equivalent to a Danish stx. Apart from English B, there are no subject, level or grade-average requirements.
EU and Nordic citizens pay no tuition; non-EU/EEA and UK citizens do. Every student pays a material fee each semester (autumn 2026: DKK 2,678 for ceramics, DKK 3,346 for glass).
In its quota 2 criteria the page names "English equivalent to a Danish A-level", but its specific admission requirement is English B. English A is a ranking factor here, not a requirement.
An IB Diploma of 24 points or more gives access to every higher education programme in Denmark, subject to programme-specific requirements.

Select 'International Baccalaureate' in the country/examination dropdown. The page was last edited 2026-01-07. Note the Agency is explicit that a full Diploma need not contain a grade of 3 in every subject — a 2 may appear where the IB's own conditions for awarding the Diploma were met. Several Danish university pages state the stricter rule; that rule applies to DP Course Results, not to a Diploma. Source corrected on 2026-09-24: the 24-point sentence is on the Agency's "Optagelse af IB-elever" guidance page, not the country/examination lookup previously cited.
IB total points convert to the Danish 7-point grade average via a table re-issued annually and published by 1 March for that summer's intake.

Danish higher education is delivered by five kinds of institution: universities, university colleges, business academies, institutions in architecture and art, and maritime educational institutions. A reform is under way affecting all of them except maritime programmes.
Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen (Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science)
Read in Danish. The rule is question 5 of the Agency’s FAQ, phrased as the exact question a student would ask.
The quota 1 cut-off (or "all qualified admitted") and the number admitted for every Danish programme in the 2026 intake.
The official mapping of IB subjects and levels onto Danish A, B and C levels, including both post-2019 mathematics courses.
IB applicants must apply by 15 March at 12:00 noon CET, whether applying in quota 1 or quota 2, and whether the IB was taken in Denmark or abroad.

The source states the day and month but not the admission year; Danish national deadlines have been stable for many years. Treated as provisional for 2027 until the Agency publishes dates carrying that year.
The 2026 SU grant for a higher-education student living away from home is DKK 7,426 per month before tax.

This is the 2026 rate. The rate for 2027 will differ, and the SU reform taking effect on 1 January 2027 reduces the total grant frame for higher education from 70 to 58 portions for anyone starting a new programme on or after 1 July 2025 — which includes this cohort.
Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen (SU)

The page attaches no academic year to this range, and its own USD, EUR and DKK figures are not mutually consistent at current rates. Usable as an order of magnitude only; the institution is the authority for its own fee.
Study in Denmark
A student budget in Denmark runs to roughly DKK 8,450–13,700 per month.

Non-EU students need a study residence permit costing DKK 3,060, must show DKK 7,426 per month of self-support, and may work 90 hours a month from September to May plus full-time in June, July and August.
SIRI's page was last updated 2026-09-15 and supersedes Study in Denmark's own pages, which still quote a retired 20-hours-a-week rule.
Danish universities must reduce academic bachelor intake by about ten per cent across 2025–2029 compared with the 2018–2022 average.

Subject list matches. The page writes "Social Science B" where the record has Social Studies B; the Danish subject is Samfundsfag in both cases and Aarhus renders it inconsistently across its own pages.
The University of Copenhagen teaches all 78 of its bachelor programmes in Danish.

DP Course Results (formerly the IB Certificate) of at least 18 points, with at least grade 3 in all six subjects and at least three subjects at HL, are a qualifying examination in Denmark on the same terms as a two-year hf without overbygning: they give access to erhvervsakademi- and professionsbachelor programmes through quota 1 and quota 2, and to a university bachelor only after two successive raises of upper-secondary subject level, at least one to A level, taken as hf-enkeltfag. Course Results under 18 points, or containing any subject at grade 1 or 2, are not a qualifying examination at all. A full IB Diploma of 24 points or more gives access to every higher education programme in Denmark.

This is the rule that decides whether a Course candidate can apply at all, and it is national: the Agency sets which examinations are adgangsgivende and every Danish institution applies the same one, so it is recorded once here and referenced from each Opportunity rather than restated per institution. No institution page read for this catalogue states it. The Agency says in as many words that IB Certificate is the former designation for DP Course Results, which is why this site uses Course Results throughout: "Samme vilkår gælder for ansøgere med IB Certificate, som er den tidligere betegnelse for Diploma Programme (DP) Course Results." The Agency’s companion FAQ at .../spoergsmaal-og-svar-om-diploma-programme-dp-course-results-og-ib-certificate-i-forhold-til-optagelse-paa-en-videregaaende-uddannelse-i-danmark/ carries the same rule as a table and adds the detail that where an A-level subject other than Danish is already held, two raises to B level suffice. Two traps. GSK is NOT a route: "en IB-elev kan ikke benytte gymnasial supplering, GSK-fag, til at hæve sit uddannelsesniveau". GSK meets a specific subject requirement for somebody who already holds a qualifying examination; the level of the examination itself is raised only by hf-enkeltfag. data/ib-conversion.json currently reads "Supplementary subjects are taken as hf-enkeltfag or GSK", which this source contradicts and which should be corrected in that file. The second trap is that a Course candidate who later supplements or retakes is still converted on the ORIGINAL Course Results average, because that was the first qualifying examination. What this record does NOT establish: whether a diplomingeniør offered by a university is admitted under the professionsbachelor order or the university order. The Agency’s guidance names programme types and this one is a professional bachelor degree awarded by a university, so the three BEng Opportunities in this catalogue are left with no entry-award rule recorded and say so on their own records.

So a Danish IB student applies to a public university through the same platform as French school-leavers. A non-EU student uses the DAP (dossier blanc via the embassy, or dossier vert if resident in France), which this site does not record as a route.

Graduates of secondary schools in EU member states, with at least one parent not of Greek descent and the last two school years completed abroad, are a sub-category of the ministry's foreign-nationals route into Greek public universities. Enrolment requires Greek at B2, certified by the University of Athens, the University of Thessaloniki or the Centre for the Greek Language; a successful applicant without it may complete enrolment in the following year's enrolment period once they have it, or loses the place. 2026-2027 enrolment ran 11 to 25 September 2026.

This answers how a Danish IB graduate gets into a Greek-taught public programme: category B1, not the Panhellenic exams. The catch is Greek at B2, needed to enrol, not to apply. Addressed to universities, ΑΣΠΑΙΤΕ, ΑΣΤΕ and the higher ecclesiastical academies, which also shows which public institutions the route covers.

The University of Iceland's application deadline page lists the autumn undergraduate deadline of 5 June under a heading for Icelandic and Nordic citizens, a group that includes a Danish citizen applying from Denmark.

Read literally, this makes 5 June the deadline for a Danish applicant, because a Danish citizen is a Nordic citizen. That reading is contradicted by the university's own FAQ, which is recorded separately as ev-hi-is-faq-5-june. This record deliberately does not resolve the two: the convenient reading here is the later deadline, and preferring it is exactly the choice that costs a student a year if it is wrong.

Read literally, this excludes a Danish applicant applying from Denmark, who has not lived in Iceland. It cannot both be true and ev-hi-is-deadline-page-5-june be true, because the two describe different groups as the one 5 June belongs to. The untranslated Icelandic "og" left in the middle of an English sentence is worth recording: it is what a partial translation that has fallen out of step with the page it contradicts looks like from the outside, and it is a reason to suspect this page is the stale one — but a suspicion is not a fact, and the product declines to state a date on the strength of it.

Which of the two a Danish citizen is held to is disputed by the university itself; see ev-hi-is-deadline-page-5-june and ev-hi-is-faq-5-june. The safe date is 1 February. Years are inferred from the intake.

The document is written for visa applicants, and most of it does not concern a Danish student: Universitaly pre-enrolment is for non-EU applicants who need a visa. What it establishes for an EU applicant is the absence of a central system — you apply on each university's own portal on its own calendar. The same circular names the sectors (università, AFAM, SSML, ITS Academy) and says ITS Academy candidates apply directly to the ITS, which is why the sector landscape cites it. It is explicitly valid for two academic years, 2026-27 and 2027-28, so it does cover autumn 2027 entry.

This is the far more useful half of the University of Tokyo story and it replaces the flat statement that Todai has closed. PEAK ended and a larger, differently shaped English-taught route opened in its place: a whole new faculty, the university's first in about seventy years, on a September intake deliberately chosen to match Europe and North America, with half its places reserved for the international route. For a Danish IB student the consequential detail is the date — applications close on 5 November 2026, six weeks after this was written, with the Route B result on 22 December 2026 and the final decision on 20 February 2027. It is the earliest deadline of any Japanese route recorded here, and it is decided entirely on predicted grades. Note also that this is a five-year integrated programme ending at master's level, not a three- or four-year bachelor's; a student comparing it with a Dutch bachelor is not comparing like with like.

The Embassy of Japan in Denmark's own scholarship pages could not be read in this pass. They are the body that sets the Danish application dates for every MEXT scholarship, and none of those dates is established here.

Recorded because the gap is consequential and because a blank field would look like an absence of a requirement rather than a failure to check. MEXT says explicitly that the application process and the specific schedule differ by country and are the embassy's to set, so the embassy is the rule-owner for the only dates a Danish student actually needs, and we could not reach it. The page exists — the block is an edge-network refusal, not a missing document — so this is a call or an email rather than another fetch. The embassy is at Havneholmen 25, Copenhagen. Nothing on this page has been read and nothing is claimed from it.
Embassy of Japan in Denmark

The Embassy of Japan in Denmark offers Danish nationals two MEXT scholarship types, Japanese Studies and Research Student, and both are for students already at university. The undergraduate scholarship is not among them.

The friendliest Japanese calendar we found for an IB candidate, and the reason is Period III. It closes on 7 April 2027, by which point a May 2027 candidate's predicted grades are settled and their mock results exist, and it announces on 24 May — still before the diploma, but after the exams. Keio also says in as many words that predicted grades are acceptable, which most Japanese programmes leave to inference. The trade is that the three periods share one quota of about 100 places, so a later period is competing for what the earlier ones did not take. Applying in Period I is the stronger position; applying in Period III is the one that fits the Danish school year.

This is the sentence that fixes a dating error this repository was carrying: a record written in September 2026 told students to contact the Embassy of Japan in Denmark 'in early 2026', which was already in the past when it was written. The rule is relative, not absolute — April and May of the year before arrival — so for an April 2028 arrival the window is April and May 2027, which is exactly when a Danish IB candidate is sitting their examinations. That collision is worth saying out loud: the MEXT application and the IB exam session fall in the same eight weeks, and the paperwork includes a health certificate and a recommendation letter that cannot be produced in a hurry. MEXT also says plainly that the exact dates are the embassy's to set, so the national page can never be the last word.

This is the single table that settles which intake a Danish IB student is actually planning for. The 1st Round is Korea's main March intake and it closed a day before this was read — an IB candidate sitting exams in May 2027 could never have used it, because they would have had to matriculate in March 2027 with no diploma. The 2nd Round is the one that fits: apply in March 2027 on predicted grades, hear in June 2027, start in September 2027, three weeks before the diploma-holding cohort would otherwise be idle for a year. Note that the 2nd Round is published only as a month, not a date, and is explicitly marked TBD. That is a real date not yet set, not a date we failed to find.

The exemption is written in terms of the country, not the language of instruction, and Denmark is not on the list. An IB Diploma taught entirely in English at a Danish gymnasium therefore does not obviously exempt the applicant, and this changed for 2027 — an applicant working from a 2026 guide would not know it had. Whether UIC accepts IB English A or B in place of a test is not stated on the page we read and should be asked of the admissions office in writing before a TOEFL or IELTS booking is skipped.

The rule-owner's own list, used here rather than an English-language summary of it, because the summaries almost always stop at 'universities' and the useful part of the list is everything after that. The junior college is Korea's answer to the question the research brief asks of every country — the institution type nobody mentions to foreigners. It is two or three years, practical, and the nearest Korean relative of the Danish erhvervsakademi. Note that polytechnic colleges sit under the labour ministry rather than this one, which is why they are missing from most education-ministry material.

Two things are recorded here and the second is as useful as the first. The first is how early Korea's most selective university closes: applications for a March 2027 start were taken over four days in July 2026, eight months ahead, with a 70,000 KRW fee. The second is that SNU's English admissions page links a document written in Korean. The cover and the file name are in English; the eligibility conditions, the document list and the schedule are not. We read the schedule table because dates and Korean numerals survive translation; we have not read the eligibility text and do not claim to have. The route an IB student from a Danish gymnasium would use is 글로벌인재특별전형 II, 'those who completed the entire curriculum overseas' — which is the twelve-years-abroad category, and is the one that takes the Suneung out of the question.

This is the correction that matters most about Korean funding, and it contradicts what this repository previously said. A Danish passport does not open the Global Korea Scholarship's embassy route at all: Denmark is absent from the quota table and there is no Korean embassy listed for it in the guidelines' own contact appendix, while Sweden and Poland are both present. Only the University Track is available to a Danish citizen, and that track is not a general scholarship — the UIC Program is science and engineering at thirteen named universities, none of them Yonsei, KAIST or Seoul National, and each applicant may choose one university and one department only. The honest summary is that GKS is a smaller opportunity for a Dane than for most nationalities, and that telling a student to 'apply through the Korean embassy in Copenhagen' sends them to a door that is not there.

Citizens of Lithuania, the EU or EFTA who completed school abroad can apply through LAMA BPO for state-funded places. IB Diploma holders do not need their subjects or grades converted; they upload the diploma. Anyone not eligible for a state-funded place applies to the institution directly for a fee-paying place.

The same page lists SEC Level 3 passes in Mathematics, English Language and Maltese and says they 'may also be satisfied through the subjects presented in the IB Diploma if such subjects are deemed comparable'. The admissions FAQs add that a non-Maltese applicant educated abroad may offer another language instead of Maltese with Admissions Board approval. Page last updated 21 April 2026.

A non-Maltese applicant educated abroad may offer another language instead of the SEC Maltese pass, with Admissions Board approval; non-Maltese M.D. applicants must instead pass the Medical Maltese Proficiency examination before the course starts.

The absence is the finding. Denmark publishes an official IB-to-Danish conversion table and every Danish cut-off is expressed in it. The Netherlands has no equivalent, because Dutch admission is not built on a converted average: you either hold a qualifying diploma or you do not, and where demand exceeds places the institution runs its own selection. A student moving between the two systems should not expect a Dutch equivalent of the Danish table to exist somewhere unfound.

Read for what it does and does not reach. The mandatory limb of lid 2 is about a DIPLOMA and cannot reach a Course Result. The Lisbon limb of lid 1 is different in kind: it turns on whether the applicant HAS ACCESS to higher education in a convention country rather than on what document they hold, and Denmark — where this site's readers sit their IB — publishes in as many words that DP Course Results of at least 18 points with grade 3 in all six subjects give access to Danish erhvervsakademi and professionsbachelor programmes. A Danish-resident Course candidate therefore has an argument under this limb that a candidate with no such access does not have. It is an argument and not an entitlement: the same sentence preserves the institution's power under article IV.1 of the convention to show a substantial difference between the access rules in the awarding country and the Dutch ones, and 'access to hbo in Denmark' against 'access to wo in the Netherlands' is exactly the kind of difference an institution may point at. No Dutch institution page read for this catalogue mentions the limb at all. It is recorded because a route that exists in the statute and is never advertised is precisely what a Course candidate cannot find alone, and it must be raised with the admissions office in writing, early, and in those terms.

This is the door the Netherlands actually publishes for someone without a qualifying diploma, and three things about it decide whether it is any use to an IB Course candidate. First, the age: twenty-one. A student who leaves school at eighteen with Course Results does not qualify for two or three years, and lid 3 makes the exceptions discretionary — the institution MAY waive the age limit, and the first of its two grounds is a foreign DIPLOMA that gives access at home, which a Course Result is not, leaving only the 'bijzondere gevallen' clause. Second, the language: the statute requires the committee to find sufficient command of DUTCH, which is a strange fit with the English-taught bachelor programmes this catalogue lists, and no institution page read for this catalogue explains how the two meet. Third, it is per programme and per institution: lid 2 puts the requirements in each programme's own onderwijs- en examenregeling, so there is no national syllabus and no national result, and passing one does not carry to another programme. None of this makes it a route a Course candidate can plan on at eighteen, and that is the finding rather than a gap in it.

This is the first non-Danish entry requirement recorded here and it is the test case for ADR 0002. The page needs no translation layer at all: it names IB subjects and IB levels, so the requirement is written as ibSubject plus ibLevel and the engine compares it with the transcript directly. Note also that TU Delft distinguishes the two IB mathematics courses by name and rejects one of them. That is why the requirement records mathematics-aa specifically, and why a 'mathematics' family shorthand would have quietly told an Applications and Interpretation student they qualified.

An IB Diploma gives general admission (generell studiekompetanse) when Norwegian and English are documented. The Norwegian requirement is met by grade 3 or better in Norwegian A, Norwegian B HL, Swedish A or Danish A at higher or standard level; English by English at grade 3 or better or English as the language of instruction.
Settles the question the profile used to leave open: a Danish IB student with Danish A meets the Norwegian requirement without a Norwegian test.

Two of these dates are the single most consequential thing on this page for a Danish candidate sitting the May 2027 session, and both fall before results exist. The mid-year route - which is the only way to start in 2027 rather than waiting until February 2028 - closes to international applicants on 8 June 2027, and closes a month later for domestic ones, so the earlier date is specifically ours. And the competitive health programmes for the following February close on 1 July 2027, days before IB results are published. Neither is a date a student would find by looking for a national deadline, because there is not one; both are a single university's dates, published on that university's own page, and the other seven universities will have their own. The lesson generalises even where the numbers do not: in New Zealand the deadline that matters is the one on the programme page, and for an international applicant it is frequently earlier than the domestic one.

Unitec lists an International Baccalaureate score of 24 or above as meeting entry to degree-level programmes, while the Danish Studentereksamen with an average of 8.0 on the 11-point scale is listed only against diploma-level programmes.

The most directly useful thing found for a Danish reader in the whole New Zealand pass, and it is on a page nobody would think to open. At this provider the Danish school-leaving certificate on its own is mapped to diploma entry, a level below a bachelor degree, while the IB Diploma is mapped to degree entry. The IB is not a marginal advantage here; it is the difference between starting a degree and starting a diploma. Two cautions: this is one provider's mapping and says nothing about the universities, and the grading scale quoted is the old Danish 13-scale wording rather than the current 7-point scale, which suggests the row has not been revised recently.
The reference to an 11-point scale does not match either Danish grading scale in current use. Worth querying with Unitec before a student relies on the Denmark row.

The finding that shapes all of Portugal for a Danish student: the English-language 'international' routes at Porto, Nova SBE and elsewhere are closed to an EU citizen. Public universities are reached through the Concurso Nacional de Acesso, at the Portuguese fee.

Católica is a private university outside the national contest, so unlike the public universities it is open to a Danish IB student directly, in English, on predicted grades. The dates are the 2026 intake's; 2027 not yet published.

Two corrections and one gap. LASALLE's degrees were validated by Goldsmiths, University of London; they are now awarded by UAS, and a record still saying Goldsmiths is describing a qualification a 2027 entrant will not receive. The same applies to NAFA. The gap is more consequential: UAS names Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents as eligible for the Tuition Grant and says nothing at all about international students, and directs the question back to LASALLE and NAFA. Whether a Danish student at LASALLE can obtain the grant — and whether they would therefore be bonded — is not established here, and must not be assumed either way from what the autonomous universities do.

The sequence is what matters and it is easy to miss: the commitment is chosen on the application form, months before anyone explains it, confirmed at offer stage in mid-July, and only signed in September or October once the student is already in Singapore with a Student's Pass and a Singpass. By the time the contract is in front of them they have flown, paid a deposit and moved in. A Danish family should treat the tick-box on the application form as the decision point, not the signature. Note also the ceiling: the grant runs for the normal duration only, so a repeated year or a change of course is paid for at the unsubsidised rate.

This is the clearest answer to the July problem anywhere in this repository, and it contains a restriction that is easy to read past. A student sitting the May 2027 session — which is the Danish IB timetable — is excluded from four NTU programmes outright, including Medicine and the Renaissance Engineering Programme, because those decide before results exist. For everything else NTU takes predicted grades and then wants the real thing within three days of release. Three days, in the first week of July, is a genuine trap for a family on holiday, and the IBO transcript access has to be granted months earlier for the result to reach NTU at all.

Singapore is often described as having no central admissions system, and for applying that is true — six universities, six forms, six fees, six deadlines. It is not true for accepting. Every offer a student holds across the autonomous universities lands in one portal and is settled in one exercise against one deadline, which is closer to the Danish or Dutch model than to the American one, and which means the choice between them is made once rather than offer by offer. Nobody tells international applicants this, and it changes how the spring is planned.
The national Study in Slovenia portal states that a candidate who finished school abroad is obliged to obtain a decision on the recognition of their foreign education, and names no exemption.
A Danish citizen applies on the Slovenian timetable, not the separate foreigners' one.

This is the whole University of California calendar and it has no early round in it. There is one thirty-day window, it closes six weeks before most American colleges close, and nothing reopens afterwards — no Early Action, no Early Decision, no rolling consideration, no equivalent of Clearing. A Danish student who treats 1 January as "the American deadline" has already missed all nine UC campuses by a month. The 15 July row is the answer to the July problem here and it is unusually generous: UC makes its offers on predicted grades and then wants the real IB results nine days after the IB releases them.

Two things a student coming from the Common App will get wrong. The fee is per campus rather than per application, so nine campuses is 855 USD for a Danish applicant and not 95. And the teacher references that dominate every other American application are not part of this one — UC decides on the academic record and four personal insight questions. A student who spends October chasing recommendation letters for Berkeley has spent October on the wrong thing.

The phrase that matters to a Dane is "reasonably accessible in your location". A Danish travel or study policy may be comprehensive and still fail, because it is not accessible in Cambridge, Massachusetts. This is also the clearest case in this Destination of a rule that is genuinely per-state rather than per-institution: it binds every institution in Massachusetts and no institution outside it, and three of the fourteen institutions in this profile are in Massachusetts. The waiver window closes in July, before a student has arrived.

The phrase to read carefully is "along with". An IB Diploma is one of the most demanding secondary qualifications in the world and at Yale it does not remove a single requirement — it sits beside the SAT, it does not replace it. For a Danish IB student this is a 2026 problem, not a 2027 one: the SAT has to be booked, sat and possibly retaken before the November round, and the decision to do that has to be taken about eighteen months before enrolment.

Worth recording for the detail almost no other page states: the application deadline and the deadline for everything that has to arrive behind it are different dates, a week apart. A Danish student whose school uploads the transcript and predicted grades is dependent on a studievejleder hitting 7 November, not 1 November, and nobody tells them that. The time zone is also published, which most are not — 23:59 Central Time is 06:59 the next morning in Denmark.

"Need-aware, then full need" is the commonest arrangement a Danish family will actually meet, and it is different from both of the things students are told about America. It is not need-blind — asking for money makes admission harder — and it is not sticker-price-only either: if they take you, they fund you. The operational point is the one about deadlines. The aid application is due the same day as the admission application, so a family that plans to "see what happens and then ask about money" has forfeited the money.

Arizona State is on this list because it is the one institution here that does not run a selection tournament — admission is against published criteria, decisions come back on a rolling basis, and a student can know roughly where they stand before applying. That makes it the realistic counterweight to a list of single-digit admit rates. Two cautions. Its fall 2027 priority date is simply not published yet, so no date has been invented for it here. And the English-proficiency requirement is stated without an IB exemption, so a Danish IB student should ask ASU in writing whether English A or B at Higher Level satisfies it rather than assuming.

"Charges no application fee" is worth more to a Danish family than it looks. A list of twelve American colleges at 75–100 USD each is close to 1,000 USD spent before a single decision arrives, and the fee waivers that soften it are built around low-income American students. Colleges that charge nothing at all change what a realistic list can contain. Colby's deadlines are not recorded here, because Colby's own pages could not be read.

This is the route almost no IB student is told exists, and it is the cheapest way into an American bachelor's degree. It is recorded from a promotion agency, which means it establishes that the route exists and how it is meant to work, and establishes nothing about price, admission or transfer at any particular institution. The mechanism that would make it real for a specific student is a published transfer guarantee such as UC's TAG (ev-uc-transfer-guarantee), and whether an F-1 student from Denmark qualifies for one on the same terms as a Californian is the open question this Destination has not answered.

A Danish student is a nonresident and stays one: residency for tuition at UC is not something an F-1 student can acquire by living in California, so the higher figure is the figure for all four years. The gap between the two rows is a little over 41,000 USD a year, and it is the whole of what "in-state versus out-of-state" means in practice — it is not a discount a foreign student can qualify into. The Tuition Stability Plan is the one piece of good news: the tuition line is fixed at entry, which is rarer in the United States than in Europe.

Automatic enrolment is the part to notice. This is not an offer a student accepts; it is a charge that appears on the bill unless a waiver is filed by a deadline, and the Danish yellow card and the EHIC are worth nothing against it. Two semesters at the 2026-27 rate is over 5,000 USD, which is more than a year's total living costs in several European destinations. The 2027-28 rate is not published yet and must not be assumed to be this one.

The sentence about IB scores is the one most likely to be misread, and misreading it costs a year. It is not an IB exemption. It is a hardship provision for applicants who cannot reach a test centre, and Copenhagen has test centres. A Danish IB student reading "IB Actual or Predicted Scores" as an alternative to the SAT will arrive at 1 November without a test score and without a way to get one. Read alongside Yale's flat refusal (ev-yale-testing-policy), the safe planning assumption for the selective American universities is that the SAT or ACT is required and has to be sat during 2026.
